Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National New Economy agenda needs clear roadmap, not just ambitious targets – Vicky Bright Source : Kareen Tei 16 November 2026 11:32am ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
International corporate lawyer and entrepreneur Vicky Bright has welcomed the NDC government's proposed 2027 New Economy agenda but says its success will depend on a clear implementation plan that translates economic growth into jobs and improved living standards.
The agenda seeks to boost local production, manufacturing, value addition and job creation, with the government targeting 8 per cent economic growth and a reduction in unemployment to 8 per cent by 2030.
Speaking on the JoyNews AM Show on Monday, November 16, Ms Bright said the targets were worth pursuing but stressed that the government must demonstrate how its policies would deliver tangible benefits to Ghanaians.
“I support the government's ambition to achieve this 8% economic growth and bring unemployment down to 8% by 2030. We need sustained growth,” she said.
“But the real question for me is how that ambition, because it's an ambition at the moment, will actually translate into opportunities and better living standards for all Ghanaians.”
She acknowledged improvements in Ghana's macroeconomic stability and said the country's renewed appeal to international investors was encouraging.
“If you look at where we were in 2024 as a nation and where we are now, and our attractiveness even to the international markets, I think people now want to invest in Ghana again,” she noted.
Ms Bright also welcomed proposed measures to strengthen local textile manufacturing, process 50 per cent of Ghana's cocoa domestically and phase out expensive emergency power arrangements.
She said the initiatives, together with plans to consolidate mineral-related investment funds to establish a sovereign wealth fund, could deliver significant economic benefits if properly implemented.
However, she cautioned that economic growth would not automatically lead to a corresponding reduction in unemployment.
“8% GDP growth does not automatically mean a corresponding reduction in unemployment,” she said.
She identified agriculture, manufacturing, tourism and technology as sectors with considerable potential to create jobs, but argued that the infrastructure and support systems needed to drive growth in these areas must be strengthened.
In agriculture, she said farmers needed access to storage facilities, reliable transportation, processing infrastructure and dependable markets for their produce.
Manufacturers, she added, required affordable electricity, working capital and accessible markets to expand their operations and employ more people.
Ms Bright also urged the government to pay attention to the quality and sustainability of jobs created, arguing that employment figures should distinguish between permanent positions, temporary construction work and training opportunities.
Ms Bright identified institutional performance and the business environment as critical to the success of the New Economy agenda.
She said businesses needed predictable tax policies, timely permits, reliable electricity and prompt payment for services delivered to the government.
She warned that delays in settling government contracts could undermine businesses' cash flow, limiting their ability to expand and create jobs.
“These everyday conditions influence whether an entrepreneur can expand and employ another 10 or 20 people, or they stay put because it's just too much,” she said.
Ms Bright also called on the government to establish measurable commitments ahead of the 2030 target, particularly milestones that could be assessed by the end of 2028.
She proposed quarterly, half-yearly and annual reviews to track progress and strengthen accountability.
“2030 extends beyond the current presidential term. Long-term planning, very welcome. That's how we should be looking at things. But we need clear commitments for what will be delivered by the end of 2028,” she said.
She maintained that the New Economy agenda could deliver significant benefits but said its credibility would depend on adequate financing, strong institutions and effective implementation.
“I support the ambition. But I think we should have a clear delivery plan,” she stressed.
